cards.body: When a child is stuck in anger or gloom and talking is getting nowhere, the authors recommend physical activity: a run round the garden, jumping, a quick game. Movement changes the state of the body, and the emotional state tends to follow, after which the child can think again. The same applies to adults. A short walk before a hard conversation is not avoidance; it is preparation.
cards.try: Next time you or a child are stuck in a bad mood, move for five minutes before trying to talk.

cards.title: Feelings are weather, not climate
cards.body: Children easily take a passing state for a permanent fact: "I'm stupid" for "I feel frustrated with this sum." The authors teach children to notice what is going on inside, including sensations, images, feelings and thoughts, and to see that these come and go like clouds. A child who learns "I feel lonely right now" instead of "I am a lonely person" has room to wait for the feeling to pass or do something about it.

books.title: Parent Effectiveness Training
books.author: Thomas Gordon
books.why: The source of active listening and I-messages, and still one of the clearest guides to family conflict.

cards.title: Whose problem is it?
cards.body: Gordon's starting question in any difficulty is who owns the problem. If the child is upset about something in their own life, such as a quarrel with a friend, the child owns it, and the parent's job is to listen. If the child's behaviour is interfering with the parent's needs, such as noise during a phone call, the parent owns it and should speak up. Much confusion comes from using the wrong skill for the situation.

cards.title: Roadblocks to listening
cards.body: When a child brings a trouble, parents usually respond with one of a dozen habits: ordering, warning, moralising, advising, lecturing, criticising, praising to cheer them up, reassuring, questioning, changing the subject. Gordon calls these roadblocks. Each, however kindly meant, tells the child that their feeling is not acceptable or that the parent will take over, and the child stops talking.

cards.title: Active listening
cards.body: In place of the roadblocks, Gordon teaches reflecting back what you understand the child to be feeling, in your own words and without judgement. "You're worried you won't be picked for the team." If you are wrong, the child corrects you; if right, they go deeper. He stresses that it only works if you really want to hear and can accept the feeling. Children listened to this way often find their own solutions.
cards.try: When someone tells you a worry today, say back the feeling you hear and add nothing else.

cards.title: I-messages
cards.body: When the parent owns the problem, Gordon recommends saying how the behaviour affects you instead of what is wrong with the child. A you-message blames: "You're so inconsiderate." An I-message describes the behaviour, its concrete effect and your feeling: "When the music is that loud I can't hear the caller, and I get frustrated." It leaves the child's dignity intact and trusts them to respond.
cards.try: Turn one complaint into the form "When ..., I feel ..., because ..." and say it calmly.

cards.title: Nobody has to lose
cards.body: Gordon rejects both the method where the parent wins by using power and the one where the child wins because the parent gives in. Power breeds resentment and rebellion; giving in breeds a child who ignores others' needs. His third way is joint problem-solving: define the conflict as needs on both sides, list possible solutions together, choose one acceptable to both, and check later that it is working. People keep agreements they helped to make.

cards.title: Values cannot be forced
cards.body: Some clashes are not about concrete effects on the parent but about values: hairstyle, friends, beliefs, tidiness of the child's own room. Gordon says the no-lose method often does not apply here, because the child sees no real harm to the parent, and that power fails worst of all. What a parent can do is live by their own values, share their views and knowledge once, as a consultant would, and then leave the choice with the child.

books.title: Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child
books.author: John Gottman with Joan DeClaire
books.why: It teaches a simple, well-studied method for helping children handle strong feelings.

cards.title: Four ways of meeting a child's feelings
cards.body: Gottman describes four parental styles. The dismissing parent treats sadness or anger as trivial and tries to distract. The disapproving parent criticises or punishes the feeling. The laissez-faire parent accepts every feeling but offers no guidance or limits. The emotion coach accepts the feeling and also helps the child understand it and decide what to do. His research found children of emotion-coaching parents tended to do better with friends and at school.

cards.title: Feelings are openings, not interruptions
cards.body: Emotion coaching begins with noticing your child's emotions, including quiet signs before they grow large, and with a change of attitude: treating a child's sadness, fear or anger as a chance to be close and to teach, not as a nuisance to end quickly. That in turn requires some awareness of your own feelings. A parent who cannot bear their own anger will struggle to stay calm near a child's.

cards.title: Listen and help find the word
cards.body: The middle steps are to listen with empathy, show that the feeling makes sense, and help the child put a name to it: jealous, embarrassed, let down. Gottman says that naming a feeling has a calming effect and gives the child a tool for the next time. This is not telling the child what they ought to feel. It is offering words for what they already feel: "It looks as if you felt left out when they started without you."
cards.try: Help a child, or yourself, find a more exact word than "upset" for a feeling today.

cards.title: All feelings allowed, not all behaviour
cards.body: The last step is setting limits while solving the problem together. The feeling is accepted fully; the harmful action is not. "You're furious that she took your toy, and I understand that. Hitting is not all right. What could you do instead?" Then the parent helps the child think of options and choose one. Without this step, empathy becomes permissiveness, which Gottman found left children less able to calm themselves.
cards.try: The next time you set a limit, say the feeling you accept first, then the behaviour you do not.

cards.title: You do not have to coach every time
cards.body: Gottman is realistic about family life. Emotion coaching is unsuitable when you are short of time, when there is an audience, when you are too upset or tired yourself, or when a child is putting on a feeling to get their way. Nor does it remove the need for discipline. He reassures parents that they need not respond perfectly on every occasion; a pattern of coaching over time is what counts.

books.title: The Explosive Child
books.author: Ross W. Greene
books.why: A humane, practical method for children whose outbursts do not respond to rewards or punishment.

cards.title: Children do well if they can
cards.body: Greene sets his view against the common belief that children do well if they want to. That belief treats a child who explodes as unmotivated, manipulative or badly raised, and answers with more rewards and penalties. Greene holds that such a child would behave better if they were able to, since doing well is always preferable. So the right question is not how to make them want to, but what is getting in their way.

cards.title: Lagging skills, not bad attitude
cards.body: In Greene's account, explosive children are behind in certain thinking skills: flexibility, tolerating frustration, shifting from one activity to another, solving problems, putting worries into words. When a situation demands a skill they lack, they fall apart, much as a child with a reading difficulty struggles when asked to read. Rewards and punishments supply motivation, which was never the missing piece, and often make matters worse.

cards.title: Outbursts are predictable
cards.body: Explosions feel sudden but usually occur under the same conditions: getting ready for school, homework, turning off a screen, a change of plan. Greene calls each of these an unsolved problem. He asks adults to list them specifically and pick a few to start with. Once you know when trouble is likely, you can work on it in advance, at a calm time, and not in the heat of the moment when nobody can think.
cards.try: Write down the three situations that most reliably lead to conflict at home. Note the time and the trigger.

cards.title: Three ways to respond
cards.body: Greene describes three plans. In Plan A the adult imposes their will, which for these children tends to set off the explosion. In Plan C the adult drops the expectation for now, deliberately, to reduce conflict while other problems are tackled. In Plan B adult and child solve the problem together. He is clear that Plan C is not giving in; it is choosing priorities, because nobody can work on everything at once.

cards.title: Solving it together
cards.body: Plan B has three steps. First, gather information about the child's concern with patient, neutral questions: "I've noticed mornings have been hard. What's up?" Second, state the adult's concern, such as getting to school on time. Third, invite the child to think of a solution that works for both, and try it. The first step takes longest, since children often need help to find out what is bothering them.
cards.try: At a calm moment, open one difficult topic with "I've noticed ... What's up?" and only listen.

cards.title: Safety and help
cards.body: Greene's method is about reducing how often a child reaches breaking point, and it works mainly between episodes. During an outburst itself, the aim is to keep everyone safe and to calm things, not to teach or negotiate. Families living with frequent, severe or violent outbursts should not carry this alone. A doctor or child mental health professional can check for underlying difficulties and support the parents as well.

books.title: The Self-Driven Child
books.author: William Stixrud and Ned Johnson
books.why: A persuasive case that children thrive when given more control over their own lives.

cards.title: A sense of control protects against stress
cards.body: The authors, a neuropsychologist and a test-preparation coach, argue that the most stressful thing for anyone is feeling they have no say over what happens to them. Children whose days are fully scheduled and supervised by adults can feel exactly that. A sense of being in charge of one's own life, they say, supports motivation and mental health. So a parent's aim is not to steer everything but to help the child build that sense.

cards.title: Be a consultant, not a manager
cards.body: A manager decides and enforces. A consultant offers knowledge and advice, and the client makes the decision. The authors suggest parents take the second role wherever they reasonably can: "Here is what I know and what I would do; I am happy to help; it is your choice." This does not mean no rules. It means recognising that you cannot make a child want something, and that pushing often produces resistance.
cards.try: Offer advice once today, then say "but it's your call" and mean it.

cards.title: "It's your call"
cards.body: The authors encourage letting children make their own decisions about their own lives once they have the relevant information, with the parent keeping a veto only for choices that most reasonable adults would consider dangerous or badly mistaken. Children will sometimes choose poorly. A poor choice with small consequences at twelve teaches more than a perfect record of decisions made by someone else, and builds judgement for the choices that come later.

cards.title: Whose homework is it?
cards.body: The book's best-known advice is about homework battles. When a parent works harder on a child's schoolwork than the child does, the child learns that someone else is responsible for it, and evenings turn into fights. The authors suggest offering help at a set time and place without nagging or forcing, and letting the school's consequences do their work. Protecting the relationship matters more than any one assignment.
cards.try: Tonight, say once "I'm here from seven to eight if you want help" and do not mention homework again.

cards.title: Be a calm presence
cards.body: Anxiety spreads within a family. A parent's worry about marks or the future passes to the child, who then has two people's fear to carry. The authors argue that one of the most useful things a parent can do is manage their own stress, so that home is a safe base and not another source of pressure. They suggest making enjoyment of your child a priority, and reminding yourself that their life is long.

cards.title: Rest is part of the work
cards.body: The authors give great weight to sleep and to unstructured downtime: daydreaming, sitting quietly, time with no screen and no task. They argue that a mind needs these periods to recover and to make sense of experience, and that tired children learn poorly and feel worse. They also remind families that there are many routes to a good life, and that one test or one school does not decide a child's future.

books.title: The Gardener and the Carpenter
books.author: Alison Gopnik
books.why: A leading child psychologist questions the idea that parents should shape children to a plan.

cards.title: "Parenting" is a recent idea
cards.body: Gopnik notes that the word parenting, as a kind of job with techniques and a product, only became common in the late twentieth century. Earlier generations spoke of being a parent, which is a relationship, not a task. She argues that the job model is a poor fit. We do not talk about wifing or friending a person in order to turn them into something. Caring for a child, she says, is a form of love, not a form of work with a measurable output.

cards.title: Carpenter or gardener
cards.body: A carpenter starts with a design and judges success by how closely the chair matches it. A gardener prepares rich soil, protects the plot and accepts that what comes up will be partly a surprise. Gopnik argues that raising children is like gardening. The evidence that particular parenting techniques produce particular adults is weak, she says, while a safe, loving, varied environment plainly lets many kinds of children flourish.

cards.title: Childhood is for exploring
cards.body: Human children stay dependent for an unusually long time. Gopnik's explanation is that this protected period lets the young explore widely and try out possibilities, while adults do the work of getting things done. Children's mess, noise and unpredictability are part of that design. A species facing changing conditions benefits from offspring who vary. Trying to make a child efficient and focused too early works against what childhood is for.

cards.title: Children learn by watching and playing
cards.body: Gopnik's own research field is how young children learn, and she reports that they pick up a huge amount simply by observing the people around them, imitating, listening and playing. Play lets them test ideas without cost. She cites studies suggesting that when an adult teaches one specific use of a toy, children explore it less. Instruction has its place, but being near capable adults doing real things is itself an education.
cards.try: Let a child join in a real task today, such as cooking or fixing something, without turning it into a lesson.

cards.title: Love without a blueprint
cards.body: If parents are not shaping a product, what are they for? Gopnik's answer is that they provide the secure, stable base from which a child can become a person nobody could have predicted, quite possibly one with different tastes and values from their parents. The commitment is to this particular child, whoever they turn out to be. That lifts an impossible burden: you are responsible for the garden, not for the exact shape of the plant.
cards.try: Name one way a child you love differs from you, and tell them what you admire about it.

books.title: The 36-Hour Day
books.author: Nancy L. Mace and Peter V. Rabins
books.why: The standard family guide to caring for someone with Alzheimer's disease or another dementia.

cards.title: The illness, not the person
cards.body: The book's foundation is that the difficult behaviour of a person with dementia comes from damage to the brain. Asking the same question again and again, accusing relatives of theft, refusing to wash: none of it is stubbornness or spite, and the person cannot stop by trying harder. Holding on to this helps a carer take things less personally and look for what set the behaviour off, instead of arguing or feeling wounded.

cards.title: When a small thing causes a storm
cards.body: The authors describe sudden over-reactions, such as weeping, shouting or striking out, when a person with dementia is faced with more than their brain can handle: too many questions, a noisy room, a task with several steps, being hurried. The advice is to stay calm, lower the demands, remove the person gently from the situation, and later work out what overloaded them so it can be avoided. Raising your voice or restraining them tends to make it worse.

cards.title: Do not argue with the damaged memory
cards.body: Explaining, correcting and reasoning assume a memory that can hold the explanation. When someone insists their long-dead mother is waiting for them, repeated correction brings fresh distress each time. The authors suggest responding to the feeling underneath, such as loneliness or worry, with reassurance, and then gently turning attention to something else. "You miss her. Tell me about her" is kinder and more effective than the facts.
cards.try: The next time a confused relative says something untrue, answer the feeling instead of correcting the fact.

cards.title: Simplify and keep a routine
cards.body: A predictable day spares a failing memory. The book recommends doing things at the same times and in the same order, keeping the home uncluttered and familiar, and breaking each task into single steps given one at a time: "Put your arm in here", then the next. Offer a choice between two things, not an open question. Let the person do whatever they still can, even slowly, because unused abilities fade faster.

cards.title: A sudden change needs a doctor
cards.body: Dementia usually worsens gradually. The authors stress that a sudden decline, such as new confusion, agitation, sleepiness or a fall in ability over hours or days, often has another cause that may be treatable: an infection, pain, a reaction to medicine, dehydration, constipation or another illness. The person may be unable to say what is wrong. Do not assume it is just the disease. Have it checked promptly by a doctor.

cards.title: The carer's health is part of the care
cards.body: The title refers to how long a carer's day feels. The authors insist that exhaustion, anger, grief and guilt are normal responses, and that a carer who collapses helps no one. They urge families to accept help early, share the work, take regular time away, join others in the same position, and see their own doctor. Deciding that home care is no longer possible is not a betrayal. Planning legal, money and safety matters early makes later choices easier.
cards.try: If you are caring for someone, ask one specific person for one specific piece of help this week.

books.title: How to Care for Aging Parents
books.author: Virginia Morris
books.why: A thorough, kind handbook for adult children facing a parent's growing need for help.

cards.title: Talk before the crisis
cards.body: Most families first discuss a parent's care in a hospital corridor, under pressure, with no idea what the parent would want. Morris urges having the conversations early, while the parent is well: where they would like to live if they could not manage alone, who should decide for them if they cannot, what matters most to them about the end of life. These talks are awkward to start, and they spare everyone much guesswork and guilt later.
cards.try: Ask a parent or older relative one gentle question about what they would want if their health changed.

cards.title: It is still their life
cards.body: When a parent grows frail, a worried child easily takes over: choosing, arranging, forbidding. Morris reminds readers that a competent adult keeps the right to make their own decisions, including ones their children think unwise, such as staying in a house with stairs. The helper's role is to offer information, options and support, and to protect dignity. Ask what they want before deciding what they need, and step in only as far as necessary.

cards.title: Get the papers in order
cards.body: The book gives much space to practical preparation. Find out where the important documents are kept and what the parent's income, insurance and debts are. See that there is a will, that someone trusted has legal authority to handle money and medical decisions if the parent cannot, and that their wishes about treatment are written down. Laws differ from country to country, so proper local advice is worth its cost. Done early, this is a kindness to the whole family.
cards.try: Find out where one key document is kept: a will, an insurance policy or a list of medicines.

cards.title: Share the load with the family
cards.body: Care usually lands on one person, often the daughter who lives nearest, while brothers and sisters stay distant or criticise. Morris advises calling a family meeting, in person or by phone, to lay out what the parent needs and divide the tasks. Those far away can handle bills, paperwork and calls, or pay for help. Ask for specific things, since general appeals are easy to ignore, and expect old rivalries to surface and need patience.

cards.title: Set limits so you can last
cards.body: Caring for a parent can go on for years, and Morris is frank that no one can do everything. She tells carers to decide what they can realistically give, say so, and use whatever help exists: relatives, neighbours, paid carers, day centres, respite care. Guilt is nearly universal and a poor guide. Keeping up your own health, work, marriage and friendships is not selfish. It is what allows you to keep showing up with patience.
cards.try: Write down one caring task you could hand to someone else, and whom you will ask.

books.title: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
books.author: Lindsay C. Gibson
books.why: It gives words to a quiet kind of childhood loneliness and a way to relate to parents more freely.

cards.title: Fed and clothed, yet lonely
cards.body: Gibson writes for adults whose parents provided for them materially but could not offer emotional closeness. Such parents are uneasy with feelings, react instead of reflecting, show little empathy and keep attention on themselves. The child grows up with a loneliness that is hard to name because nothing visibly went wrong. Her term, emotionally immature, comes from clinical practice and is a description, not a medical diagnosis.

cards.title: Four kinds of immature parent
cards.body: The book sketches four types. Emotional parents are ruled by their moods and make the family anxious and watchful. Driven parents are busy and controlling, always improving everyone. Passive parents are pleasant but avoid anything hard and do not protect the child. Rejecting parents want to be left alone and treat the child as a bother. Real people mix these. The sketches help a reader recognise a pattern, not sort relatives into boxes.

cards.title: The fantasy that they will change
cards.body: Children of such parents commonly form what Gibson calls a healing fantasy: a private belief that if only they were good enough, successful enough or helpful enough, the parent would at last become warm. To earn that, they adopt a role in the family in place of their real self. As adults they may carry both into other relationships, working hard to win love from people who are not able to give it.

cards.title: Internalisers and externalisers
cards.body: Gibson describes two ways children cope. Internalisers believe that solving problems is up to them: they are sensitive, self-reliant, over-responsible and inclined to do most of the emotional work in any relationship. Externalisers act before thinking, blame others and expect someone else to fix things. Most readers of the book, she says, are internalisers, whose task is to stop taking on what was never theirs to carry.

cards.title: Observe instead of hoping
cards.body: For dealing with the parent now, Gibson suggests stepping back mentally and observing, as a calm researcher might, instead of getting pulled into the old reactions. Go into each meeting with a specific, realistic aim, such as saying one thing clearly or keeping the visit pleasant, and judge it by that aim. State your thought once and let it go, without needing the parent to understand or agree. The aim is your own freedom, not their transformation.
cards.try: Before your next difficult family call, decide on one small, realistic aim and judge the call only by that.

cards.title: Distance is allowed
cards.body: Gibson does not tell readers they must stay close to a parent, or must cut one off. She says each person may decide how much contact is good for them, and that less contact is a legitimate choice when visits reliably leave them hurt. Understanding why a parent is limited is not an obligation to put up with mistreatment. Where a parent is abusive or threatening, the priority is your safety and support from a professional or others you trust.
